config.title: Same Tree

intro.title: Same Tree
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that checks if two binary trees are identical in structure and node values. You will learn the core concept of tree traversal, specifically using a depth-first search approach to compare nodes. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, conditional logic, and recursion to navigate the tree nodes. This beginner-friendly exercise will help you understand fundamental tree operations and recursive lesson-solving in algorithms.
intro.usecase: The Same Tree algorithm is essential in software that manages hierarchical data structures, such as file systems, document outlines, or organizational charts. For example, when a cloud storage service needs to verify that two folder structures are identical before syncing, or when a project management tool compares two versions of a task hierarchy to detect changes. Developers implement this pattern in UI components like tree views in file explorers, nested comment threads, or configuration panels where structural consistency must be validated. Understanding how to compare tree structures efficiently helps build reliable features for version control systems, database indexing, and any application dealing with nested data relationships.

objectives: Implement a recursive function to compare two binary tree structures.
Apply base case logic to handle null nodes in both trees.
Construct a depth-first traversal to check node values and subtrees.
Manipulate boolean return values to propagate equality results up the call stack.
Initialize a function that accepts two tree root nodes as parameters.
Integrate value comparison with recursive subtree checks in a single return statement.
Control the recursion flow to return false immediately upon finding any mismatch.

content.body: Have you ever looked at two family trees and wondered if they're identical? In coding, we often need to compare tree structures. Let's learn how to check if two binary trees are exactly the same by exploring their branches systematically.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Apply tree traversal to compare nodes
2. Implement a recursive solution for Same Tree
3. Explain why the base case matters
4. Determine when two trees are structurally identical
5. Handle edge cases like empty trees
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at these two small trees. How would you check if they're identical? Start at the root and think about what to compare.
content.title: Try it
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: Now imagine trees with 3-4 levels. Would you check all left branches first, then right? Or go level by level? Which order feels most natural?
content.title: Go deeper
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: You naturally started at the roots and worked your way down the branches. This is the essence of tree traversal - exploring from the root outward, checking each node as you go.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When trees get deeper with many branches, keeping track of what you've compared becomes challenging. How do you ensure you don't miss any nodes? How do you know when to stop exploring a branch?
content.title: Why it gets tricky

content.body: Think of exploring a tree like following paths in a forest. You start at the root (the entrance), then explore one branch at a time. For each branch, you check if the paths match in both trees before moving deeper. The base case is when you reach the end of a branch (empty tree).
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Use branch/root visual reasoning; visiting nodes or exploring levels one at a time.

content.body: We'll use depth-first search with recursion. At each node, we check: 1) Are both nodes null? (base case) 2) Are values equal? 3) Recursively check left and right subtrees. This explores branches completely before moving to sibling branches.
content.title: The approach
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body:
1. Start at the roots of both trees
2. If both are null → return true (empty trees are identical)
3. If one is null but other isn't → return false (structure differs)
4. If values don't match → return false
5. Recursively check left subtrees
6. Recursively check right subtrees
7. Return true only if both recursive checks pass
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Define the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called isSameTree that takes two tree nodes p and q as parameters.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function name(parameter1, parameter2)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you have both parameters p and q.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that accepts two tree nodes.

steps.title: Handle base cases
steps.instruction: Add the base cases: if both p and q are null, return true. If only one is null, return false.
steps.hint: Use if statements to check for null values. Remember: null means empty tree/node.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've handled the empty tree cases correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your conditions. We need two separate if statements.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's think about the base cases. What does it mean when both trees are empty?

steps.title: Compare node values
steps.instruction: Now check if the current nodes' values match. If they don't, return false.
steps.hint: Access node values with p.val and q.val. Add this after the null checks.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Use !== to check if values are different.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need to compare p.val and q.val. If they're different, the trees can't be identical.

steps.title: Recursive calls
steps.instruction: Make recursive calls to check the left and right subtrees. Store the results in variables.
steps.hint: Call isSameTree recursively for left children (p.left, q.left) and right children (p.right, q.right).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we're exploring both branches recursively.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your parameter names. Left children are p.left and q.left.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check both subtrees. Remember: each node has left and right children.

steps.title: Return final result
steps.instruction: Return true only if both left and right subtrees are identical. Use the variables you created.
steps.hint: Both leftSame and rightSame must be true for the entire trees to be identical.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've completed the Same Tree algorithm!
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. What should we return if both subtrees are identical?
steps.feedbackWrong: Think about it: both left and right subtrees must be identical for the whole trees to match.

content.body: Excellent work! You've implemented the Same Tree algorithm using depth-first traversal. Remember: always check base cases first (empty trees), compare current nodes, then recursively explore branches. This pattern of 'check current, then explore children' applies to many tree lessons. Keep practicing exploring trees branch by branch!
